journal_name: ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications and Applications

abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel theoretical framework for cross-modal multimedia retrieval based on unified information geometry. Traditional approaches treat different media modalities as separate embedding spaces, requiring complex alignment procedures. We propose the Unified Manifold Representation Theory (UMRT), which establishes that semantic content across text, image, video, and audio modalities naturally resides on a single low-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Our theoretical analysis proves that optimal cross-modal retrieval corresponds to geodesic distance minimization on this manifold, and we derive closed-form solutions for the projection operators that map arbitrary modalities to this unified space. Furthermore, we introduce the Semantic Curvature hypothesis, demonstrating that semantic similarity between multimodal queries and targets is directly proportional to the manifold curvature at their intersection points. Experiments on MS-COCO and Flickr30k datasets validate our theory, achieving 78.3% mAP on cross-modal retrieval tasks, a 23% improvement over state-of-the-art methods. This framework fundamentally reconceptualizes how we model relationships between heterogeneous media types, providing a principled mathematical foundation for next-generation multimedia retrieval systems.

We present a significantly improved theoretical model for perceptual video quality assessment that addresses critical limitations in existing no-reference (NR) metrics. Current NR video quality models rely on either hand-crafted features with limited generalization or deep features that lack interpretability. Our Hierarchical Perceptual Quality Theory (HPQT) introduces a multi-scale temporal-spatial framework that models human visual attention and quality perception across frame, shot, and scene levels. We formally prove that video quality perception follows a weighted temporal integration principle, where recent frames and scene transitions receive disproportionately higher perceptual weights. Based on this theory, we derive an analytical quality prediction function that combines spatial texture degradation, temporal discontinuity, and encoding artifact visibility. The theoretical analysis establishes that optimal quality prediction requires modeling both local frame-level impairments and global temporal context effects. Evaluations on LIVE and CSIQ video databases demonstrate that HPQT achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.89 with subjective scores, outperforming existing NR metrics by 12-18% while maintaining computational efficiency. This work provides a more principled and accurate approach to automated video quality monitoring in multimedia streaming applications.

This paper introduces EdgeMedia, a groundbreaking edge computing platform for real-time multimodal video analysis that fundamentally rethinks the architecture of distributed multimedia processing. Unlike traditional cloud-centric approaches that suffer from latency and bandwidth constraints, EdgeMedia leverages a novel hierarchical fog-cloud continuum with adaptive model partitioning. The system introduces three key innovations: (1) a dynamic computation graph partitioning mechanism that distributes deep learning inference across edge devices, fog nodes, and cloud servers based on real-time resource availability; (2) a cross-modal fusion engine that processes synchronized video, audio, and sensor data streams with guaranteed temporal consistency; and (3) a context-aware model adaptation framework that continuously optimizes model complexity based on scene complexity and user requirements. EdgeMedia implements a publish-subscribe middleware supporting 50ms end-to-end latency for video analytics queries. Deployment across 12 edge nodes in a smart campus environment processes over 10,000 video streams simultaneously, achieving 94% accuracy while reducing cloud bandwidth consumption by 67% compared to centralized approaches. This paradigm shift enables new applications in autonomous driving, industrial monitoring, and smart cities where real-time multimedia understanding is critical.

We present AdaptiveCodec, a significantly improved adaptive video streaming system that addresses the challenge of delivering high-quality video under highly variable network conditions. While existing adaptive bitrate (ABR) algorithms optimize for either quality or stability, they fail to handle the emerging scenarios of 8K video, mobile edge computing, and 5G networks with ultra-reliable low-latency requirements. AdaptiveCodec introduces two major system innovations: first, a neural network-based lookahead optimizer that predicts future network conditions and video characteristics 10 seconds ahead, enabling proactive bitrate selection rather than reactive adaptation. Second, a perceptual quality optimization module that dynamically allocates bits across spatial, temporal, and quality dimensions based on content characteristics and display properties. The system implements a lightweight client-side agent trained via reinforcement learning that learns to navigate complex network dynamics while maximizing perceptual quality. Experiments across 8 diverse network traces demonstrate that AdaptiveCodec achieves 23% higher average quality of experience (QoE) scores while reducing quality fluctuations by 41% compared to state-of-the-art methods like Pensieve. The system maintains smooth playback under network jitter up to 40% while preserving sharp detail in high-motion scenes, representing substantial improvements in practical multimedia streaming performance.
